### C-R3-01
**Claim:** Chapter 5 is a new start: the scroll reverts to attacking Jerusalem/Judah on life and unfaithful relationship with Yahweh that make Yahweh’s action necessary; it confronts a people in denial.
**Quote:** “Chapter 5 makes for a new start as the scroll reverts to a focus on attacking Jerusalem and Judah concerning its life and its unfaithful relationship with Yahweh, which make it necessary for Yahweh to act. It confronts a people in denial.”
**Locus:** slice ~167–169 (intro to ch. 5 / section D)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R3-02
**Claim:** Goldingay’s summary of ch. 5’s charges: faithless interpersonal relations; resistance to Yahweh’s discipline; faithlessness toward Yahweh; resistance to warnings; accumulation of stuff by deceit and denying the needy rights; prophets, priests, and people collude — therefore invasion/devastation is threatened, though Yahweh will not wipe them out.
**Quote:** “They are faithless in their relationships with one another. … They accumulate stuff by deceit and by denying needy people their rights. Prophets, priests, and people collude in following this lifestyle. Yahweh therefore threatens them with invasion and devastation, though he will not wipe them out.”
**Locus:** slice ~171–185
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R3-03
**Claim:** Strings of imperatives at 5:1, 10, and 20 mark three sections of similar length (vv. 1–9, 10–19, 20–31); 6:1 begins another unit that is more warning than confrontation.
**Quote:** “Strings of imperatives appear in vv. 1, 10, and 20, and I have yielded to the temptation to treat these as the beginnings of sections. They thus initiate three sections of similar length, vv. 1–9, 10–19, and 20–31. Another set of imperatives begins in 6:1, marking the beginning of another unit; they constitute more warnings than confrontations.”
**Locus:** slice ~187
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R3-04
**Claim:** Ch. 5 bulk can be read against Jer 36 (604 scroll) as reformulation of messages over ~twenty years; some material may be later; in exile it could justify Jerusalem’s fall, but is not originally designed that way — it says Yahweh has acted, not finally, and focuses on action still to come.
**Quote:** “The bulk of the chapter can again be read against the background of the story in Jer 36, but once more it will be a reformulation by Jeremiah of messages given over the previous twenty years… In the context of the exile, it could function to justify Yahweh’s action in letting Jerusalem fall, but it is not expressed as if originally designed to fulfill this function.”
**Locus:** slice ~187
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R3-05
**Claim:** Throughout ch. 5, speakers shift (Yahweh / Jeremiah / aides) but it is always Jeremiah speaking even when as Yahweh, and Yahweh’s message even when Jeremiah speaks in his own name; readers ask how Jeremiah’s experience functions as Yahweh’s message.
**Quote:** “It is always Jeremiah speaking, even when he speaks as Yahweh, and it is Yahweh’s message even when Jeremiah speaks in his own name. Readers of the scroll have to ask, how does this account of something that Jeremiah experienced function as Yahweh’s message?”
**Locus:** slice ~189
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

## 1. Universal Deceptiveness (5:1–9)

### C-R3-06
**Claim:** Yahweh commissions agents to investigate whether any faithful people are in Jerusalem; none among ordinary people; Jeremiah investigates the important people and finds none; that explains the necessity to strike rather than pardon; one stage of striking has happened, further action must follow.
**Quote:** “Yahweh (by implication) commissions agents to investigate whether there are any faithful people in Jerusalem. There are none among the ordinary people, so Jeremiah goes off to investigate the important people and also finds none among them. That discovery explains the necessity for Yahweh to strike them down rather than pardon them.”
**Locus:** slice ~302–302 (section prose before structure outline)
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R3-07
**Claim:** The investigative commission (šûṭ polel “go about”) fits heavenly aides like Gen 18’s two who check Sodom; overlaps with Sodom and with Isa 1’s Jerusalem-as-Sodom language (acknowledging, authority, truthfulness, rebellion, children, whoring, etc.).
**Quote:** “But if we should seek to identify them, they will be his heavenly aides, like the two in Gen 18 who go to check things out in Sodom. There are overlaps between this section and that story; it might also remind listeners of Isa 1…”
**Locus:** slice ~328
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R3-08
**Claim:** “Exercising authority” and “seeking truthfulness” are the vocation of those responsible for justice; nowhere in the city do people with power operate in a way that respects truth; Yahweh looks for someone like Moses/Aaron/Phinehas/Samuel — if one such person exists, pardon becomes possible.
**Quote:** “Yahweh is then not looking for just an ordinary individual but for someone like Moses, Aaron, Phinehas, or Samuel—someone who is pushing the city to live in a way that matches his concern for faithfulness. If there is such a person, then all is not lost. It opens up the possibility of pardon.”

**Quote:** “Pardoning (sālaḥ) differs from forgiving (nāśāʾ). Forgiving means a person who has been wronged ‘carries’ the consequences of the wrong action… Pardoning means a person with authority stops treating a rebel or transgressor as a rebel or transgressor.”
**Locus:** slice ~330

## 2. The Foreign Service (5:10–19)

### C-R3-17
**Claim:** Section structure: commission of hard pruning (10–13); Yahweh puts devastating words in Jeremiah’s mouth (14–18); explanation that punishment fits the crime (19); may juxtapose originally separate subsections.
**Quote:** “The section again begins with a command to take disciplinary action in light of the falsehood of Ephraim and Judah, continues with words to Jeremiah that spell out the implications of the action, reassures the listeners that it will not be the end, and adds a rationale implying that the punishment will fit the crime.”
**Locus:** slice ~453
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R3-18
**Claim:** Commission to devastate vineyard-terraces but “do not make an end” (echo 4:27); remove tendrils that “do not belong to Yahweh” — disowning, not total uprooting; comparable to Paul’s savage vine-lopping in Rom 9–11; working out of determination in 5:9.

## E. Mostly (Final) Warning (6:1–30) — Structure / End of Part 1

### C-R3-33
**Claim:** 5:31’s “What will you do at the end?” could have closed the 604 scroll, but Jer 6 climaxes the opening chapters: looks back, tightens the screw, concludes the nightmare vision with a “massive announcement of disaster” — a paradigm “horror text.”
**Quote:** “The question ‘What will you do at the end of it?’ (5:31) could have served nicely as a conclusion to the 604 scroll, but it is Jer 6 that brings the Jeremiah scroll’s opening chapters to a climax. … conclude the nightmare vision in the collection of messages with a ‘massive announcement of disaster.’ It is a paradigm ‘horror text.’”
**Locus:** slice ~686
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R3-34
**Claim:** Goldingay’s five-part outline of ch. 6: (1–8) flee *from* Jerusalem (ironic revisit of 4:5–9); (9–15) strip remains of vine, wrath pours indiscriminately; (16–21) worship unacceptable, Yahweh trips them; (22–26) northern invader as horrifying reality; (27–30) chilling retrospective on 1:18 commission. After first section, each begins “Yahweh has said this” (except v. 27).
**Quote:** “vv. 1–8 … fleeing to Jerusalem will not work: it is necessary to flee from Jerusalem … vv. 27–30 Yahweh engages in a chilling retrospective on the fulfilling of Jeremiah’s commission in 1:18 … After the first section, each section begins with a form of the declaration ‘Yahweh has said this.’”
**Locus:** slice ~689–719
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

## 1. Sanctify a Battle / Battle-Terror (6:1–8)

### C-R3-35
**Claim:** Ironic reverse of 4:6: Benjaminites must make safe *from inside* Jerusalem — capital is especially unsafe; Jeremiah himself a Benjaminite; Tekoa (paronomasia with “blast”) and Beth Hakkerem (possibly Ramat Rahel fortification) get alarm; dire trouble from the north peers out (šāqap) — past tense of certainty; “great shattering” repeats 4:6 but Zion is no longer refuge.
**Quote:** “First he urges Benjaminites to make safe by getting themselves or their people out of Jerusalem, with irony since many would have taken refuge there because they thought it was safe and because 4:6 had issued a commission to get people to take refuge in Zion… No, even Jerusalem is not safe; actually, it is especially not safe, because it’s the capital.”
